questions.q: Why does the migration script take pg_advisory_xact_lock(4242) first?
questions.explain: Two servers may start the migration at the same time. The lock makes the second one wait; when it gets the lock, it sees the migration is already recorded and skips it.
options: To stop users from reading tasks during the migration
So two copies of the script started at the same moment wait for each other instead of both applying the same migration
To encrypt the migration
To make the migration faster

questions.q: This simulates the migration script run twice. What does it print?
questions.explain: Migrations that are already recorded are skipped, so running the script a second time is safe and only prints database is up to date. That is what lets you run it on every deployment.

applied migration 1
applied migration 2

questions.q: The migration script runs every migration inside BEGIN … COMMIT, with ROLLBACK in the catch. What happens if migration 2 fails?
questions.explain: With a transaction the run is all or nothing. You fix the migration and run the script again, instead of repairing a half-changed database by hand.
options: Migration 1 stays applied and migration 2 is half done
Everything in the transaction is undone, so the database is left as it was before the run
The script retries migration 2 forever
The failed migration is marked as applied

questions.q: On the server you run npm ci --omit=dev. What does it do?
questions.explain: npm ci follows the lock file exactly, so the server gets the same versions you tested. --omit=dev leaves out tools that production never needs.
options: Installs the newest version of every package
Installs exactly the versions in package-lock.json, without development tools such as TypeScript, tsx and Vitest
Compiles the TypeScript code
Deletes node_modules and exits

questions.q: Which ports should the firewall of your Linux server allow from the internet?
questions.explain: PostgreSQL's 5432 is never open to the internet. The app itself is reached through the proxy on 80 and 443, and SSH uses 22 with a key, not a password.
options: 22, 80, 443 and 5432, so you can reach the database
Only 22 (SSH), 80 and 443 (web)
All ports, and let the app decide
Only 3000, where the app listens

questions.q: Why does the lesson create a separate system user taskapi with no login and no admin rights?
questions.explain: Least privilege: the app never runs as root. A bug in the app then cannot change system files or read other users' data.
options: systemd cannot run programs as root
If an attacker takes over the app, they get only that user's small rights, not the whole server
So the app can read every user's home folder
Because Node.js refuses to run as root

questions.q: In the unit file, what does Restart=on-failure with RestartSec=5 do?
questions.explain: A crash no longer means downtime until someone notices. The app comes back by itself after 5 seconds.
options: Restarts the app every 5 seconds
If the process crashes, systemd starts it again after 5 seconds
Restarts the whole server when the app fails
Stops the app after 5 failures

questions.q: The runtime's graceful shutdown can take up to 30 seconds. Why does the unit file set TimeoutStopSec=40?
questions.explain: After SIGTERM, systemd waits TimeoutStopSec and then kills the process. The platform's wait must be longer than the app's shutdown, or requests in flight are cut off.
options: To make deployments take longer
So systemd waits longer than the app's own shutdown before it kills the process
So the app restarts after 40 seconds
Because systemd requires a value over 30

questions.q: The secrets are in /etc/task-api/env. Which permissions does the lesson set?
questions.explain: Only root and the app need the secrets. Any other user on the server, or a process that breaks out of another service, cannot read them.
options: chmod 777, so the app can surely read it
chmod 640 and chown root:taskapi: root can write it, the app's group can read it, nobody else can
chmod 644, readable by every user on the server
No permissions: the file is committed to Git instead

questions.q: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
questions.explain: You build an image once with a Dockerfile, then start as many containers from it as you need, on your laptop, in CI and on the server.
options: An image runs on Linux, a container runs on Windows
An image is the package of the app and everything it needs; a container is a running copy of an image
They are two words for the same thing
A container is built from a Compose file, an image from a unit file

questions.q: Why does the Dockerfile use a multi-stage build?
questions.explain: In the lesson the build stage installed 85 packages and the final stage only 30. The 55 development tools never reach the image you ship.
options: So the image can run two apps at once
The final image gets only the compiled code and production packages, not the build tools
So that npm ci runs twice for safety
Because Docker cannot run tsc in the final image

questions.q: Why does the Dockerfile copy package.json and package-lock.json before src?
questions.explain: A step is rebuilt only when its inputs change. Dependencies change rarely, code changes often, so copy the dependency files first and the source code after.
options: Docker needs them to find the source code
Docker caches each step, so when only the code changes, npm ci is not run again and the build takes seconds
It makes the image smaller
So the lock file overwrites the source code

questions.q: Why is CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] written in the list form?
questions.explain: With the list form there is no shell in between, so the stop signal reaches Node.js directly and the graceful shutdown runs.
options: The list form runs faster
So node itself receives SIGTERM and can shut down gracefully
So the app can read .env
Docker does not accept any other form

questions.q: Which file must .dockerignore keep out of the image, above all?
questions.explain: Anyone who gets the image could read files inside it. Secrets are passed as environment variables when the container runs, never baked into the image.
options: package.json
tsconfig.json
.env, with your secrets
src

questions.q: This splits an image reference into a name and a tag. What does it print?
questions.explain: An image with no tag means latest, which tells you nothing about the version. Deploy with version tags such as task-api:1.0.0 so you know what runs and can go back.

questions.q: Inside Docker Compose, why does the app connect to db:5432?
questions.explain: This is the DNS-based service discovery from the microservices lesson. The name db keeps working even when the database container is replaced.
options: Because db is PostgreSQL's default host name
Compose puts the services on a private network where each one reaches the others by its service name
Because port 5432 is published to the internet
Because Caddy forwards database traffic

questions.q: In the lesson's compose.yaml, only the proxy service has ports. Why?
questions.explain: Every request goes through the proxy and its HTTPS. Publishing the app or the database directly would let people go around it.
options: The other images do not support ports
The app, database and Redis are reachable only inside the Compose network, never from the internet
Ports cost money on a server
Because Redis would crash with a port

questions.q: What happens to the database if the db service has no volume for /var/lib/postgresql/data?
questions.explain: Volumes keep data when containers are replaced. That is also why docker compose down --volumes must never run on a real server: it deletes them.
options: Nothing, containers always keep their data
The data lives inside the container and is lost when the container is replaced, for example on a deployment
PostgreSQL refuses to start
The data is copied into the image

questions.q: This mimics Compose's ${NAME:?message} rule. What does it print?
questions.explain: :? means "required": with no value, the start stops with the message. There is no default password, so a forgotten secret can never silently become an empty or weak one.

required variable POSTGRES_PASSWORD is missing a value: set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env

postgres://taskapi:p4ss@db:5432/taskapi

postgres://taskapi:undefined@db:5432/taskapi
postgres://taskapi:p4ss@db:5432/taskapi

required variable POSTGRES_PASSWORD is missing a value: set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env
required variable POSTGRES_PASSWORD is missing a value: set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env

questions.q: The URL class can read a DATABASE_URL. What does this print?
questions.explain: protocol keeps its colon, hostname has no port, and pathname starts with /, so slice(1) gives the database name. Never print url.password.
questions.code:
const url = new URL("postgres://taskapi:s3cret@db:5432/taskapi");
console.log(url.protocol, url.hostname, url.port, url.pathname.slice(1), url.username);
options: postgres: db 5432 taskapi taskapi
postgres db 5432 /taskapi taskapi
postgres: db:5432 5432 taskapi s3cret
postgres: localhost 5432 taskapi taskapi

questions.q: You want to log which database the app uses without leaking the password. What does this print?
questions.explain: Setting url.password replaces only the password part, and * is allowed there as it is. The host and database name stay readable for debugging.
options: postgres://taskapi:***@db:5432/taskapi
postgres://taskapi:s3cret@db:5432/taskapi
postgres://***@db:5432/taskapi
postgres://taskapi:%2A%2A%2A@db:5432/taskapi

questions.q: The lesson stops the database. What do /health and /ready answer?
questions.explain: The app is alive but cannot serve, so nothing restarts it and traffic stops going to it. When the database starts again, /ready answers 200 by itself.
options: Both 503
Both 200
/health 200 and /ready 503
/health 503 and /ready 200

questions.q: You replace :80 in the Caddyfile with api.example.com. What does Caddy then do by itself?
questions.explain: It needs the DNS record in place and ports 80 and 443 open. Add a volume for /data so the certificates survive a restart.
options: Nothing until you install certbot
Gets a free TLS certificate from Let's Encrypt, renews it, redirects HTTP to HTTPS and adds the Strict-Transport-Security header
Moves the app to another server
Buys the domain for you

questions.q: Why must you never set trustProxy: true on an app that is also reachable directly?
questions.explain: Believe the forwarded address only from your own proxy: "loopback" when nginx runs on the same machine, "private" inside Docker.
options: The app would stop answering HTTPS requests
Anyone can send an X-Forwarded-For header, so an attacker could pick their own IP address and walk around your per-IP rate limit
It makes the app slower
Caddy refuses to connect to it

questions.q: This picks the client IP the way a trusted-proxy check does. What does it print?
questions.explain: The first request came from Caddy on the private Docker network, so its forwarded address is believed. The second came straight from the internet with a forged header, so the app uses the real socket address.

questions.q: What is the order of the deployment steps in the lesson?
questions.explain: The backup comes first so you can recover from a bad migration. Migrate before replacing, keep the old image tag, and watch /ready, the logs and the dashboard afterwards.
options: Replace the app, then migrate, then back up
Back up, build a new tag, migrate, replace the app, check
Migrate, back up, replace, build
Build, replace, check, and back up only if something breaks

questions.q: You want to rename the column title to name. Why split it into two deployments (expand and contract)?
questions.explain: Deployment 1 adds name, copies the data and writes both. Deployment 2, when no old code is left, removes title. It also keeps rolling back to the previous image possible.
options: Because PostgreSQL cannot rename columns
Between migrating and replacing the app, the old app still runs against the new database, so every migration must work with both versions
So the deployment takes longer
Because migrations can change only one column per day

questions.q: A migration that already ran in production has a mistake. What should you do?
questions.explain: The old migration is recorded as applied, so an edited version never runs there, and other environments end up different. A new migration fixes every database the same way.
options: Edit that migration file and run the script again
Add a new migration that fixes it
Delete the row from schema_migrations and run it again
Fix the table by hand in psql

questions.q: During the rename, the new code writes both columns. What does this print?
questions.explain: Because the new code writes both columns, the old code still sees correct data while both versions run. Only in the second deployment is title removed.
options:
Write docs | Write docs
Write the deploy guide | Write the deploy guide

Write docs | undefined
Write the deploy guide | Write the deploy guide

Write docs | Write docs
Write docs | Write the deploy guide

undefined | Write docs
Write the deploy guide | Write the deploy guide

questions.q: "A backup you have never restored is only a hope." How does the lesson prove a backup works?
questions.explain: Only a restore shows that the file really contains your data. Then the scratch database is dropped. Test a restore regularly, not only once.
options: By checking that the file is larger than 0 bytes
By restoring it with pg_restore into a scratch database and reading the rows back
By running pg_dump twice and comparing the files
By opening the .dump file in a text editor

questions.q: Where should nightly backups be stored?
questions.explain: A backup on the same server dies with the server. Keep several copies (for example 7 daily, 4 weekly, 12 monthly) away from it, encrypted.
options: In the backups folder on the same server
Somewhere else, such as encrypted object storage in another region
In the Git repository
In the Docker image

questions.q: What does docker compose down --volumes do, and where must you never run it?
questions.explain: It is the clean-up command for your own computer. On a production server it deletes the production data.
options: Stops the containers only; it is safe anywhere
Removes the containers, the network and the volumes with the database; never run it on a real server
Makes a backup of the volumes; run it every night
Restarts the containers with fresh images; run it on every deployment

questions.q: A Compose service has image: task-api:latest, ports: "3000:3000" and DATABASE_URL: postgres://admin:admin123@db:5432/taskapi. Which is not one of its problems?
questions.explain: db is correct: Compose resolves service names. The real problems are the latest tag, the published port, and a weak, hard-coded superuser password.
options: latest hides which version runs and makes going back hard
Port 3000 publishes the app around the proxy and its HTTPS
The password is weak, written in the file, and belongs to an admin user
The database host db is wrong and must be an IP address

questions.q: A crontab line starts with five time fields. What does this print for 30 2 * * *?
questions.explain: The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. 30 2 * * * means 02:30 on every day: the nightly backup time in the lesson's practice.
options: at 02:30 every day
at 30:02 every day
at 02:30 some days
at 2:30 some days

questions.q: This keeps backups for 14 days, like find backups -mtime +14 -delete. What does it print?
questions.explain: Only files older than 14 days are removed, so the 14-day-old file stays. Old backups are deleted automatically, but copies outside the server keep your longer history.

[ 'taskapi-2026-09-22.dump' ]
[ 'taskapi-2026-09-01.dump' ]
[ 'taskapi-2026-09-01.dump', 'taskapi-2026-09-09.dump', 'taskapi-2026-09-22.dump' ]

questions.q: How much log space does the lesson's logging option allow per container?
questions.explain: parseInt("10m", 10) reads the leading digits, 10. Three files of 10 MB is at most 30 MB; older lines are dropped.
options: 30 MB
13 MB
10 MB
NaN MB

questions.q: Finish missingVars(env, names). Return the names whose value is missing or empty, joined with ", ", or "ok" when none are missing. The program should print DATABASE_URL, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and then ok.
questions.explain: Like Compose's ${NAME:?…}, an empty value counts as missing. Report every missing name at once, never the values.

questions.q: Finish parseDatabaseUrl(raw) with the URL class. Return { host, port, database, user }: port as a number (use 5432 when the URL has none), database without the leading /. Do not return the password. The program should print the two objects shown in the comment.
questions.explain: url.port is a string, and an empty one when the URL has no port. Leaving the password out means the result is safe to log.
questions.expected:
{ host: 'db', port: 5432, database: 'taskapi', user: 'taskapi' }
{ host: 'localhost', port: 6543, database: 'shop', user: 'app' }

questions.q: Finish readiness(checks). Each check is an async function that returns true or throws. Run every check; return { status: 200, body: { status: "ready" } } if all passed, otherwise { status: 503, body: { status: "not ready" } }. Do not put the error message in the body. The program should print 503 not ready and then 200 ready.
questions.explain: A failed check means 503, so the proxy stops sending traffic. The error message contains an internal address, which is why it goes to the logs, never into the public response.

questions.q: At startup the app waits for the database with retries. Finish backoffSchedule(attempts, base, max): return the wait before each retry, doubling from base and never above max. The program should print [ 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 2000 ].
questions.explain: Doubling gives the database time to start without hammering it; the cap keeps the waits short. depends_on with service_healthy helps too, but the app should still cope with a slow database.

questions.q: Finish pending(migrations, appliedIds). Return the ids of migrations not yet applied, in order. The program should print [ 3, 4 ] and then [].
questions.explain: This is the heart of the migration script: skip what schema_migrations already records. An empty list is why a second run only prints "database is up to date".

questions.q: The platform waits waitMs after SIGTERM, then kills the process. What does this print?
questions.explain: With TimeoutStopSec=40, systemd waits longer than the runtime's 30 s, so shutdown finishes. A 10 s wait is shorter, so a slow shutdown would be cut off: keep the app's timeout below the platform's wait.

systemd: clean shutdown
docker default: killed mid-shutdown

systemd: clean shutdown

docker default: killed mid-shutdown

docker default: clean shutdown

questions.q: In a crontab, % has a special meaning. What does this print?
questions.explain: In the JavaScript string "\\%" is a backslash followed by %, so each % becomes \%, as a crontab needs. The date is filled in by the shell when the job runs, not now.
questions.code:
const command = "pg_dump -U taskapi -d taskapi --format=custom > backups/taskapi-$(date +%F).dump";
console.log("30 2 * * * " + command.replaceAll("%", "\\%"));
options: 30 2 * * * pg_dump -U taskapi -d taskapi --format=custom > backups/taskapi-$(date +\%F).dump
30 2 * * * pg_dump -U taskapi -d taskapi --format=custom > backups/taskapi-$(date +%F).dump
30 2 * * * pg_dump -U taskapi -d taskapi --format=custom > backups/taskapi-$(date +\\%F).dump
30 2 * * * pg_dump -U taskapi -d taskapi --format=custom > backups/taskapi-2026-09-23.dump
